div.head: Pax 1
div.ab: Ðus feor sceal beon þæs cinges grið fram his burhgeate, þær he is sittende, on feower healfe his, ðæt is III mila ⁊ III furlang ⁊ III ǽcera bræde ⁊ IX fóta ⁊ IX scæftamunda ⁊ IX berecorna.

(De pace in curia regis.) Tam longe debet esse pax regis á porta sua, ubi residens erit, a quatuor partibus: hoc est tribus miliariis et III quarentenis et III acris in latum et IX ped. et IX granis ordei.

[Pax regis.] So weit soll der [örtliche] Sonderfriede des Königs reichen, vom Thore seiner Burg, wo er derzeit residirt, aus nach dessen vier Richtungen [überall] hin: nämlich 3 Meilen und 3 ‘Furchenlängen’ und 3 ‘Ackerbreiten’ und 9 Fuss und 9 ‘Schafthände’ und 9 Gerstenkörner.

[The king's peace.] So far shall the king's [local] special peace extend from the gate of his stronghold where he is residing, in [all] his four directions: namely 3 miles and 3 ‘furrow-lengths’ [furlongs] and 3 ‘acre-breadths’ and 9 feet and 9 ‘shaft-hands’ and 9 barley-corns.

The king's peace must be so far from his gate, where he will be residing, from four parts [on all sides]: this is three miles and 3 furlongs and 3 acres in width/broad and 9 feet and 9 thumbs and 9 grains of barley [one inch].
div.note: U: translator unrecorded: check; The Latin is the Quadripartitus; Liebermann's Old English is from H (Textus Roffensis f. 38, after V As, same hand, c. 1120; perhaps a fragment of a law). H reads ‘Ðis III’ with ‘æt’ written above. ‘grið’ is borrowed from the North, so after c. 910; Liebermann dates Pax c. 910–c. 1060. Liebermann's notes: an English mile is nearly ¼ German mile; a furlong is ⅛ English mile; an acre-breadth is 1/10 furlong, about 66 feet; a shaft-hand (fist with raised thumb) is about ½ foot. The Quadripartitus heading ‘(De pace in curia regis.)’ is only in MS R, in red. Clause number 1 added (this text has a single clause).; F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date in the running heads), October 2026 (was “c.910–c.1060 ; ?mid-990's (Wormald)”, now “c.910–c.1060 (Liebermann); ?mid-990s (Wormald)”); F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date at the head of the text); Wormald, Making of English Law I; Whitelock, English Historical Documents I, October 2026 (was “c.910–c.1060 (Liebermann); ?mid-990s (Wormald)”, now “c.910–c.1060 (Liebermann, I p. 390); ?mid-990s (Wormald, MEL pp. 371–2)”); BQ: page of each of Liebermann’s texts and of his German, checked against Liebermann, Gesetze I (our double-read transcription), October 2026 (e.g. was “(empty)”, now “H 390; Q 391; German 391”; 1 rows of Pax)

I have prefixed these two words only in order to be able to cite the piece under the catchword Pax

Der Q-Verfasser, zusammenhängend mit Heinrichs I. Staatsverwaltung und Hofgericht, wollte vielleicht den Sonderschutz von der Person und Ortsnähe des Königs hinüberziehen auf die Regierung und deren Beamte und diesen so eine Sicherheit aus altehrwürdigem Rechte beilegen

The author of Q, who was connected with Henry I's state administration and court, perhaps wished to transfer the special protection from the person of the king and his immediate vicinity to the government and its officials, and so to confer on them a security derived from time-honoured law

Bessere Übs.: ‘[als Richter?] sitzt’. Für sittan ist neben ‘wohnen, weilen’ die Bed. ‘als Herrscher, in Würde vorsitzen, thronen’, dagegen nicht ‘als Richter sitzen’ belegt. So bleibt fraglich, ob ‘Burgtor’ hier, wie allerdings in Geþyncðo 2, speziell mit dem Richtersitz zu verbinden ist

A better translation: ‘sits [as judge?]’. For sittan, besides ‘dwell, stay’, the meaning ‘preside as ruler, in state, be enthroned’ is attested, but not ‘sit as judge’. It therefore remains doubtful whether ‘burh-gate’ is here to be connected specifically with the judge's seat, as it admittedly is in Geþyncðo 2
